title: Part 4, Chapter 5
paragraphs: When Raskolnikov arrived at the investigating office at eleven the next morning, as requested, he was surprised at being kept waiting so long—at least ten minutes before he was called in. He had expected them to pounce on him at once. Instead he stood in the waiting room while people who apparently had nothing to do with him passed to and fro. In the next room, which looked like an office, several clerks sat writing, clearly without the slightest notion of who Raskolnikov was. He looked around uneasily and suspiciously for some guard, some watch being kept to prevent his escape. But there was nothing of the sort—only the faces of clerks absorbed in petty paperwork, and other people, none of whom seemed to care about him at all. He could go wherever he liked, for all they cared. The conviction grew stronger that if yesterday's enigmatic man, that phantom sprung from the earth, had truly seen everything, they would not have let him stand here waiting. Would they have sat around until he chose to appear at eleven? Either the man hadn't yet given his information, or he simply knew nothing, had seen nothing—and so everything that had happened yesterday was once again a phantom, inflated by his sick and overstrained imagination. This theory had begun forming the day before, amid all his alarm and despair. Thinking it all over now and preparing for a fresh confrontation, he suddenly realized he was trembling—and a rush of indignation swept over him at the thought that he was trembling with fear at facing that hateful Porfiry Petrovitch. What he dreaded above all was meeting that man again; he hated him with an intense, bottomless hatred and feared that his hatred might betray him. His indignation was so fierce that the trembling stopped at once. He steeled himself to go in with a cold, arrogant bearing and vowed to say as little as possible, to watch and listen, and for once to master his overstrained nerves. At that moment he was called in.

He found Porfiry Petrovitch alone in his study. It was a room of moderate size, furnished with a large writing desk before a sofa upholstered in checkered fabric, a bureau, a bookcase in the corner, and several chairs—all government-issue, polished yellow wood. In the far wall was a closed door, presumably leading to other rooms. When Raskolnikov entered, Porfiry immediately closed the door behind him and they were alone. He greeted his visitor with an apparently warm and good-humored air, though after a few minutes Raskolnikov detected a certain awkwardness, as though Porfiry had been thrown off balance or caught in something private.

"Ah, my dear fellow! Here you are—in our domain!" Porfiry began, extending both hands. "Come, sit down, old man—or maybe you don't like being called 'my dear fellow' and 'old man'—tout court? Please don't think I'm being too familiar. Here, on the sofa."
Raskolnikov sat down, keeping his eyes fixed on him. "In our domain," the apologetic fussing, the French phrase tout court—all characteristic signs.

"He held out both hands but didn't actually give me one—pulled it back in time," Raskolnikov noted suspiciously. They were watching each other, but the instant their eyes met, they looked away quick as lightning.
"I brought you this paper—about the watch. Here it is. Is it all right, or should I copy it again?"

"What? A paper? Yes, yes, don't worry—it's fine," Porfiry said as though in a hurry, and after saying it he took the paper and looked at it. "Yes, perfectly fine. Nothing else needed," he declared with the same rapidity, and set the paper on the table.
A minute later, while talking about something else, he picked it up again and transferred it to his bureau.

"I believe you said yesterday you wanted to question me formally about my acquaintance with the murdered woman?" Raskolnikov began. "Why did I add 'I believe'?" flashed through his mind. "Why am I so uneasy about having said 'I believe'?" came a second flash. And he suddenly felt that his anxiety, from the mere contact with Porfiry, at the first words, at the first glances, had swelled in an instant to monstrous proportions. This was terribly dangerous. His nerves quivered; his agitation mounted. "This is bad! I'll say too much again."

"Yes, yes, yes! There's no hurry, no hurry," Porfiry muttered, pacing around the table without any apparent aim, darting now toward the window, now toward the bureau, now back to the table—at one moment avoiding Raskolnikov's suspicious stare, the next standing still and looking him straight in the face.
His fat, round little figure looked very strange—like a ball rolling from side to side and bouncing back.

"We've plenty of time. Do you smoke? Have you your own? Here—a cigarette!" he offered. "I'm receiving you here, you know, but my quarters are through there—my government quarters. I'm living elsewhere for the time being; some repairs needed doing here. Almost finished now. Government quarters are a wonderful thing, you know. What do you think?"
"Yes, a wonderful thing," Raskolnikov answered, looking at him almost ironically.

"A wonderful thing, a wonderful thing," Porfiry repeated, as though suddenly thinking of something quite different. "Yes, a wonderful thing!" he almost shouted, suddenly fixing his eyes on Raskolnikov and stopping just two steps away.
This stupid repetition was absurdly at odds with the grave, brooding, enigmatic look he turned on his visitor.
But it only spurred Raskolnikov's defiance, and he couldn't resist a reckless, ironic challenge.

"Tell me," he said, looking at Porfiry almost insolently and taking a kind of pleasure in his own boldness, "is it true that there's a sort of legal tradition—a technique in all investigating work—of starting from a distance, with some trivial or irrelevant topic, to encourage the person being questioned, or rather to distract and disarm his caution, and then suddenly to deal him a knockout blow with the real question? Isn't that so? It's supposed to be a sacred tradition, mentioned in all the textbooks of the art."
"Yes, yes. So you think that's why I was going on about government quarters?"

And as he said this, Porfiry screwed up his eyes and winked. A good-humored, crafty look passed over his face. The wrinkles on his forehead smoothed out, his eyes narrowed, his features broadened, and he suddenly broke into prolonged, nervous laughter, shaking all over and looking Raskolnikov straight in the face. Raskolnikov forced himself to laugh too, but when Porfiry, seeing him laugh, erupted into such a guffaw that he turned almost purple, Raskolnikov's disgust overcame all caution. He stopped laughing, scowled, and stared at Porfiry with hatred while the deliberately prolonged laughter continued. The lack of caution was on both sides, however: Porfiry Petrovitch was clearly laughing in his visitor's face and seemed utterly unconcerned by the annoyance it caused. To Raskolnikov, this was highly significant. He realized that Porfiry hadn't been embarrassed before either—that perhaps he, Raskolnikov, had walked into a trap; that something unknown to him lay beneath this, some motive; that perhaps everything was already in place and about to crash down upon him.
He went straight to the point, rose from his seat, and took his cap.

"Porfiry Petrovitch," he began resolutely, though with considerable irritation, "yesterday you expressed a wish that I come here for some inquiries"—he stressed the word "inquiries." "I've come, and if you have questions, ask them. If not, allow me to leave. I have no time to waste—I have to be at the funeral of that man who was run over, whom you also know about," he added, immediately annoyed at the addition, then more irritated at his own irritation. "I'm sick of all this, do you hear? It's partly what made me ill. In short," he practically shouted, feeling that the remark about illness was even more out of place, "in short, either examine me or let me go, immediately. And if you examine me, do it in proper form! I won't have it otherwise. So for now, goodbye—we clearly have nothing more to discuss."

"Good heavens! What do you mean? What should I question you about?" Porfiry cackled, his tone instantly changing as he stopped laughing. "Please don't worry," he began fussing about, making Raskolnikov sit down. "There's no hurry, it's all nonsense. I'm very glad you've come at last. I think of you as a visitor, nothing more. As for my awful laughing, I do apologize, Rodion Romanovitch—that is your name, isn't it? It's my nerves. You tickled me with that witty remark. Sometimes I shake with laughter for half an hour straight, like a rubber ball. I live in fear of a stroke. Do sit down, please—or I'll think you're angry."
Raskolnikov said nothing. He listened and watched, still scowling angrily. He did sit down, but kept hold of his cap.

"I must tell you one thing about myself, dear Rodion Romanovitch," Porfiry continued, moving around the room and again avoiding his visitor's eyes. "I'm a bachelor, you know, an insignificant fellow, unused to society. Besides, I've got nothing ahead of me—I'm set in my ways, going to seed. And have you noticed, Rodion Romanovitch, that in our Petersburg circles, when two intelligent people meet who aren't close but respect each other—like you and me—it takes them half an hour to find a topic of conversation? They sit there tongue-tied, feeling awkward. Everyone else has things to talk about—ladies, for instance, people of high society always have their subjects, c'est de rigueur. But people of the middle sort like us, thinking people, are always tongue-tied and uneasy. Why is that? Whether it's because we lack public spirit or because we're too honest to deceive each other, I don't know. What do you think? But do put down your cap—it looks as though you're about to leave. It makes me uncomfortable. And I'm so delighted to have you here."
Raskolnikov put down his cap and went on listening silently, with a serious, frowning face, to Porfiry's vague and empty chatter. "Is he really trying to distract me with this drivel?"

"I can't offer you coffee here, but why not spend five minutes with a friend?" Porfiry rattled on. "And these official duties—please don't mind my pacing about, excuse me, dear fellow. I'm terrified of offending you, but exercise is absolutely vital for me. I'm always sitting and glad for any chance to move about for five minutes. Sedentary life, you know. I keep meaning to join a gymnasium—they say officials of all ranks, even privy councillors, skip rope there. Science marches on! But as for my duties here, interrogations and such formalities—you yourself mentioned inquiries just now—I assure you, these sessions are sometimes more embarrassing for the examiner than for the examined. You made that observation yourself, very aptly and wittily." Raskolnikov had made no such observation. "One gets in a muddle! A complete muddle! One keeps harping on the same note, like a drum! There's supposed to be a reform—we'll get a new title, at least, he-he-he! And as for our legal tradition, as you so wittily called it, I thoroughly agree with you. Every suspect, even the most ignorant peasant, knows they start by distracting you with irrelevant questions and then deliver the knockout blow, he-he-he—your apt phrase, he-he! So you really thought my talk about government quarters was meant to—he-he! You're an ironic man. Well, I'll stop! Oh, by the way, yes—one word leads to another. You mentioned formality, about the inquiry. But what's the use of formality? In many cases it's nonsense. A friendly chat sometimes yields far more. One can always fall back on formality later, believe me. And really, what does it amount to? An investigating officer can't be bound by formality at every turn. The work of investigation is, so to speak, a free art in its own way, he-he-he!"

Porfiry paused for breath. He had simply been spouting one empty phrase after another, dropping a few enigmatic words and then reverting to incoherence. He was practically running around the room, moving his fat little legs faster and faster, staring at the ground, right hand behind his back, left hand making gestures that were absurdly out of keeping with his words. Raskolnikov suddenly noticed that as he darted about, Porfiry seemed to pause twice near the door, as though listening.
"Is he expecting something?"

"You're certainly quite right," Porfiry began gaily, looking at Raskolnikov with extraordinary simplicity—which startled him and instantly put him on guard. "Quite right in laughing at our legal methods, he-he! Some of these elaborate psychological techniques are extremely ridiculous, and perhaps useless, if one sticks too rigidly to the forms. Yes. I'm speaking of forms again. Well, if I recognize—or more strictly speaking, suspect—someone of being a criminal in a case entrusted to me, you're reading law, of course, Rodion Romanovitch?"
"I was."

"Well, here's a precedent for the future—not that I'd presume to instruct you, after your published articles on crime! No, I simply state it as a fact: if I consider this man or that one a criminal, why should I trouble him prematurely, even if I have evidence? In one case I may be obliged to arrest immediately, but in another case the situation may be quite different, you see. So why not let the man walk about town for a bit? He-he! I see you don't quite follow, so I'll give you a clearer example. If I lock him up too soon, I may actually give him—so to speak—moral support, he-he! You're laughing?"
Raskolnikov was far from laughing. He sat with compressed lips, his feverish eyes fixed on Porfiry.

"Yet that's exactly how it is, with certain types especially—because people are so different. You say 'evidence.' Well, there may be evidence. But evidence, you know, can usually be read two ways. I'm an investigating officer—a weak man, I confess. I'd like to construct a proof as clear as two times two—a direct, irrefutable demonstration! If I shut him up too soon, even if I'm convinced he's the man, I may actually deprive myself of the means of gathering further evidence against him. How? By giving him, so to speak, a defined position, a fixed status. I set his mind at rest, and he retreats into his shell. They say that at Sevastopol, right after the Battle of Alma, the clever people were terrified the enemy would attack at once and take the city by storm. But when they saw the enemy preferred a regular siege, they were delighted and reassured—it would drag on for two more months at least! You're laughing—you don't believe me? Of course you're right. You're right. These are all special cases, I admit. But note this, dear Rodion Romanovitch: the general case, the case for which all legal forms and rules are designed, doesn't actually exist, because every case, every crime, the moment it occurs, becomes a completely unique case—sometimes unlike anything that's gone before. Truly comic cases of that sort arise. Now, if I leave a certain man entirely alone, don't touch him, don't bother him, but let him know—or at least suspect—every moment that I know everything and am watching him day and night, and if he lives in continual suspicion and terror, he's bound to lose his head. He'll come to me of his own accord, or maybe do something that makes it as plain as two times two—it's delightful. It can happen with a simple peasant, but with someone of our kind—an intelligent, cultivated man, cultivated on a certain side—it's a dead certainty. Because, my dear fellow, it matters enormously to know on which side a man is cultivated. And then there are nerves—nerves, which you've overlooked! They're all sick, nervous, irritable! And how they suffer from spleen! That, I assure you, is a gold mine for us. And it doesn't trouble me at all, his walking around free! Let him, let him walk about for now! I know I've caught him and that he won't escape. Where could he go? He-he! Abroad, maybe? A Pole will escape abroad, but not our man—especially since I'm watching and have taken measures. Into the depths of the country, perhaps? But peasants live there—real, rough Russian peasants. A modern cultivated man would sooner go to prison than live among such strangers. He-he! But that's all trivial, superficial. It's not just that he has nowhere to run—he is psychologically unable to escape me, he-he! What a phrase! By a law of nature, he can't escape, even if he had somewhere to go. Have you seen a moth around a candle? That's how he'll keep circling around me, closer and closer, and then—flop! He'll fly straight into my mouth and I'll swallow him. Very amusing, he-he-he! You don't believe me?"
Raskolnikov made no reply. He sat pale and motionless, still staring into Porfiry's face with the same intensity.

"A good lesson," he thought, going cold. "This is beyond cat and mouse, like yesterday. He can't be showing off his power for no reason, teasing me—he's far too clever for that. He must have another purpose. What is it? It's all bluster, my friend—you're trying to scare me! You have no proof, and the man I saw yesterday doesn't exist. You simply want to rattle me, get me worked up in advance and then crush me. But you're wrong—you won't succeed! But why give me such a broad hint? Is he banking on my shattered nerves? No, my friend, you're wrong. You won't do it, even if you've set some trap. Let's see what you've got."

And he braced himself for a terrible, unknown ordeal. At times he wanted to spring at Porfiry and strangle him. His anger was what he had feared from the start. He felt his parched lips were flecked with foam, his heart pounding. But he was still determined to say nothing until the right moment. He realized this was the best strategy: instead of talking too much, he would irritate his adversary by his silence and perhaps provoke him into speaking too freely. At least, that was what he hoped.

"No, I see you don't believe me—you think I'm playing a harmless joke," Porfiry began again, growing livelier, chuckling constantly and pacing the room once more. "And of course you're right. God gave me a figure that can only provoke comic thoughts in others. A buffoon! But let me tell you, and I repeat, excuse an old man, dear Rodion Romanovitch—you are still a young man, in your first youth, so to speak, and so you prize intellect above all, like all young people. Clever wit and abstract argument fascinate you. That's exactly like the old Austrian Hofkriegsrath, as far as I can judge military matters: on paper they beat Napoleon and took him prisoner, cleverly working it all out in their study—but then General Mack surrendered with his entire army, he-he-he! I see, I see, Rodion Romanovitch, you're laughing at a civilian taking examples from military history! But I can't help it—it's my weakness. I love military science. And I'm terribly fond of all military histories. I've certainly missed my true calling. I should have been in the army! I might not have been a Napoleon, but I could have been a major, he-he! Well, I'll tell you the whole truth, my dear fellow, about this special case: actual reality and a man's temperament are weighty matters, and sometimes they defeat the sharpest calculations! Listen to an old man—I'm speaking seriously, Rodion Romanovitch"—as he said this, the barely thirty-five-year-old Porfiry actually seemed to age; even his voice changed and he seemed to shrink—"moreover, I'm a candid man. Am I candid or not? What do you think? I believe I truly am: I'm telling you these things for nothing, without even expecting a reward, he-he! Well, to continue: wit, in my opinion, is a splendid thing—an ornament of nature and a consolation of life—and the tricks it can play! So that sometimes a poor investigating officer barely knows where he stands, especially when his own imagination runs away with him too—he is only human, after all! But the criminal's temperament saves the day, worse luck for him! But young people, carried away by their own cleverness, don't consider that 'when they overstep all obstacles,' as you put it so wittily yesterday. The man in question—the special case, the incognito—will lie, and lie brilliantly, in the cleverest way. You'd think he'd triumph and enjoy the fruits of his wit—but at the most interesting, the most critical moment, he'll faint! Illness and a stuffy room may play their part, of course, but still! He gave us the idea! He lied incomparably but didn't reckon on his own temperament. That's what betrays him! Or he'll be carried away by his playful wit into mocking the man who suspects him—he'll turn pale, as if deliberately, to mislead, but the pallor will be too natural, too convincing—and again, he's given us an idea! The examiner may be fooled at first, but he'll think differently the next day, if he's not a fool. And it's like that at every step! The man puts himself forward where he's not wanted, talks when he should keep silent, weaves in all sorts of allegories, he-he! Comes and asks: 'Why didn't you arrest me sooner?' He-he-he! And this happens with the cleverest people, the psychologists, the literary men! Temperament reflects everything like a mirror! Look into it and admire what you see! But why are you so pale, Rodion Romanovitch? Is the room stuffy? Shall I open the window?"
"Oh, don't bother, please!" Raskolnikov cried, and suddenly burst out laughing. "Please don't bother!"
Porfiry stopped facing him, paused a moment, and then burst out laughing too. Raskolnikov stood up from the sofa, abruptly cutting short his own hysterical laughter.

"Porfiry Petrovitch," he said loudly and distinctly, though his legs trembled and he could barely stand, "I see clearly at last that you actually suspect me of murdering that old woman and her sister Lizaveta. Let me tell you, for my part, that I'm sick of this. If you believe you have the right to prosecute me, to arrest me—then do it. But I will not be mocked to my face and tormented—"
His lips trembled, his eyes blazed with fury, and his voice broke loose.
"I won't stand for it!" he shouted, bringing his fist down on the table. "Do you hear me, Porfiry Petrovitch? I won't stand for it!"
"Good heavens! What is this?" Porfiry cried, apparently genuinely alarmed. "Rodion Romanovitch, my dear fellow, what's the matter?"
"I won't stand for it!" Raskolnikov shouted again.
"Hush, dear man! They'll hear—they'll come in! Just think, what could we say to them?" Porfiry whispered in horror, bringing his face close to Raskolnikov's.
"I won't stand for it, I won't stand for it!" Raskolnikov repeated mechanically, but he too had dropped to a sudden whisper.
Porfiry turned quickly and ran to open the window.

"Some fresh air! And you need water, my dear fellow—you're ill!" He was heading for the door to call for some when he found a carafe of water in the corner. "Here, drink a little," he whispered, rushing over with it. "It'll do you good."
Porfiry's alarm and solicitude were so natural that Raskolnikov fell silent and began watching him with wild curiosity. He did not take the water, however.
"Rodion Romanovitch, my dear fellow, you'll drive yourself out of your mind, I assure you! Drink some water, do!"
He pressed the glass on him. Raskolnikov raised it mechanically to his lips, but set it on the table with disgust.

"Yes, you've had a little episode. You'll bring back your illness this way, dear fellow," Porfiry clucked with sympathetic concern, though he still looked rather shaken. "Good heavens, you must take better care of yourself! Dmitri Prokofitch came to see me yesterday—I know, I know, I have a nasty, ironic temperament, but what they made of it! Good heavens, he came yesterday after you'd left. We had dinner, he talked and talked, and all I could do was throw up my hands. Did he come on your behalf? But do sit down, for mercy's sake!"
"No, not from me. But I knew he went to you, and I know why," Raskolnikov answered sharply.
"You knew?"
"I knew. What of it?"

"Why, this: that I know more about you than just that, Rodion Romanovitch. I know about everything. I know how you went to take a flat that night, when it was dark, and how you rang the bell and asked about blood, so that the workmen and the porter didn't know what to make of it. Yes, I understand your state of mind at that time. But you'll drive yourself mad this way, upon my word! You'll lose your head! You're full of generous indignation at the wrongs you feel you've suffered, first from fate and then from the police, and so you rush from one reckless thing to another, trying to force everyone to speak out and put an end to it, because you're sick of all this suspicion and foolishness. That's right, isn't it? I've guessed how you feel? Only that way you'll lose not just your own head but Razumihin's too—he's too good a man for this situation, you must realize. You're ill, and he's good-hearted, and your illness is contagious. I'll tell you more when you're in a better state. But do sit down, for God's sake! Rest—you look terrible."

Raskolnikov sat down. The shivering had stopped; he burned all over. In amazement he listened with strained attention to Porfiry, who seemed genuinely concerned. But he didn't believe a word, though he felt a strange pull to believe. Porfiry's unexpected revelation about the apartment visit had completely stunned him. "How can it be—he knows about the flat," he thought, "and he tells me himself!"

"Yes, in our legal practice there was a case almost exactly like this—a case of morbid psychology," Porfiry went on quickly. "A man confessed to murder and kept it up! It was a complete hallucination: he produced facts, imposed on everyone—and why? He had been partly, though only partly and accidentally, the cause of a murder, and when he realized he'd given the murderers their opportunity, he sank into despair. It preyed on his mind, turned his brain; he began to imagine things and convinced himself he was the killer. But finally the High Court of Appeal reviewed the case, and the poor man was acquitted and placed in proper care. Thanks to that court! Tut-tut-tut! So, my dear fellow, you'll drive yourself into delirium if you have the urge to act on your nerves—going around ringing bells at night and asking about blood! I've studied all this morbid psychology in my practice. A man is sometimes tempted to jump from a window or a bell tower, and bell-ringing works the same way. It's all illness, Rodion Romanovitch! You've been neglecting your health. You should see an experienced doctor—what good is that fat fellow? You were lightheaded! It was all delirium!"
For an instant everything went spinning before Raskolnikov's eyes.
"Is it possible," flashed through his mind, "that he's still lying? He can't be, he can't be." He pushed the thought away, sensing what fury it could drive him to—fury that might drive him mad.
"I was not delirious! I knew exactly what I was doing!" he cried, straining every faculty to penetrate Porfiry's game. "I was perfectly lucid—do you hear?"

"Yes, I hear and understand. Yesterday too you insisted you weren't delirious—you were particularly emphatic about it! I understand everything you can tell me! But listen, Rodion Romanovitch, my dear fellow: if you really were a criminal, or somehow mixed up in this damnable business, would you insist that you were not delirious but in full possession of your faculties? And so emphatically and persistently? Would that even be possible? Quite impossible, in my view. If you had anything on your conscience, you'd be far better off insisting you were delirious. That's logical, isn't it?"
There was something sly in that question. Raskolnikov shrank back on the sofa as Porfiry leaned over him, and stared at him in silent bewilderment.
"And another thing, about Razumihin—you ought to have claimed he came on his own initiative, concealing your part in it! But you don't conceal it. You actually stress that he came at your urging."
Raskolnikov had not done so. A chill went down his spine.

"You keep lying," he said slowly and weakly, twisting his lips into a sickly smile. "You're trying again to show that you know my whole game, that you know everything I'll say beforehand," he said, aware that he wasn't weighing his words carefully enough. "You want to frighten me—or you're simply laughing at me."
He continued to stare as he said this, and again his eyes blazed with intense hatred.
"You keep lying," he said. "You know perfectly well that the best strategy for a criminal is to tell the truth as closely as possible—to conceal as little as possible. I don't believe you!"

"What a wily person you are!" Porfiry tittered. "No catching you—you're a perfect monomaniac. So you don't believe me? But you do believe me a quarter of the way already, and I'll soon make you believe the whole, because I have a genuine liking for you and sincerely wish you well."
Raskolnikov's lips trembled.

"Yes, I do wish you well," Porfiry went on, touching Raskolnikov's arm gently. "You must look after your illness. Besides, your mother and sister are here now. You ought to think of them, comfort them—instead, all you do is frighten them."
"What's that to you? How do you know about it? What business is it of yours? You're watching me and want me to know it?"

"Good heavens! I learned it all from you yourself! In your excitement you tell me and everyone else everything. From Razumihin I learned some interesting details yesterday too. No, you interrupted me, but I must point out that for all your cleverness, your suspiciousness makes you lose your common sense. Take the bell-ringing, for example. I, an investigating officer, have handed you this priceless clue—a real fact—and you see nothing in it! If I had the slightest suspicion of you, would I have acted that way? No—I'd first have disarmed your suspicions, kept quiet about what I knew, diverted your attention, and then delivered the blow: 'And what were you doing, sir, at ten or nearly eleven at the murdered woman's flat? Why did you ring the bell? Why did you ask about blood? And why did you invite the porters to go with you to the police station?' That's how I should have acted if I suspected you in the slightest. I should have taken a formal statement, searched your lodging, perhaps arrested you. So clearly I have no suspicion of you, since I've done none of that! But you can't look at it rationally. You see nothing, I say again!"
Raskolnikov flinched so visibly that Porfiry could not fail to notice it.
"You're lying all the time!" he cried. "I don't know your purpose, but you're lying! You didn't talk this way just now, and I can't be mistaken!"

"Lying?" Porfiry repeated, apparently stung, but keeping his good-humored, ironic expression and seeming not the least concerned about Raskolnikov's opinion. "Lying? But how did I treat you just now—I, the investigating officer? Prompting you with every possible defense: illness, delirium, injury, depression, the police officers, all of it! Though, to be sure, all those psychological defenses cut both ways: illness, delirium, 'I don't remember'—that's all very well, but why, my dear sir, in your illness and delirium, were you haunted by precisely those delusions and not others? There might have been different ones, mightn't there? He-he-he!"
Raskolnikov looked at him with haughty contempt.

"In short," he said loudly and imperiously, rising to his feet and pushing Porfiry back slightly as he did so, "in short, I want to know: do you consider me entirely free from suspicion, or not? Tell me, Porfiry Petrovitch, tell me once and for all—and quickly!"

"What a trial you are!" Porfiry cried, with a perfectly good-humored, sly, and composed face. "And why do you want to know? Why do you need to know so much, when no one has even begun to bother you? You're like a child begging for matches! And why are you so anxious? Why do you force yourself on us? He-he-he!"
"I repeat," Raskolnikov cried furiously, "I can't put up with it any longer!"
"With what? The uncertainty?" Porfiry interrupted.
"Don't mock me! I won't have it! I tell you I won't have it. I can't and I won't—do you hear!" he shouted, slamming his fist on the table again.

"Hush! Hush! They'll overhear! I'm warning you seriously—take care of yourself. I'm not joking," Porfiry whispered. But this time his face bore no trace of its usual old-womanish good nature and alarm. Now he was commanding, stern, frowning—for once dropping all pretense.
But this lasted only an instant. Raskolnikov, bewildered, suddenly fell into genuine frenzy—but strangely, he once again obeyed the command to speak quietly, though he was in a paroxysm of fury.

"I will not be tortured," he whispered, instantly recognizing with hatred that he could not help obeying, which drove him to even greater fury. "Arrest me, search me, but act in proper form! Don't play with me! Don't you dare!"
"Don't worry about form," Porfiry interrupted with his old sly smile, gloating, as it were, over Raskolnikov. "I invited you quite informally, in a friendly way."
"I don't want your friendship and I spit on it! Do you hear? Now watch: I'm taking my cap and leaving. What will you say if you mean to arrest me?"
He seized his cap and went to the door.
"But won't you see my little surprise?" Porfiry chuckled, again catching him by the arm and stopping him at the door.
He seemed to grow more playful and good-humored, which drove Raskolnikov wild.
"What surprise?" he asked, standing still and looking at Porfiry in alarm.
"My little surprise—sitting right there, behind the door, he-he-he!" He pointed to the locked door. "I locked him in so he wouldn't escape."
"What is it? Where? What are you—"
Raskolnikov went to the door and tried to open it, but it was locked.
"It's locked. Here's the key!"
And he produced the key from his pocket.
"You're lying!" Raskolnikov roared, losing all restraint. "You lie, you damned Punch!" And he rushed at Porfiry, who retreated to the other door, not at all alarmed.
"I see through it all! You're lying and mocking me so I'll betray myself—"
"Why, you could hardly betray yourself further, dear Rodion Romanovitch. You're beside yourself. Don't shout—I'll call the clerks!"

"You're lying! Call them! You knew I was ill and tried to drive me into a frenzy to make me give myself away—that was your plan! Produce your facts! I see through everything! You have no evidence—nothing but miserable, worthless suspicions, Zametov's guesswork! You knew my character; you wanted to push me to fury and then stun me with priests and deputies! Are you waiting for them? What are you waiting for? Where are they? Bring them out!"

"What deputies, my good man? What an imagination! And it wouldn't even be proper procedure, as you said yourself. You don't know the rules, dear fellow. But procedure can wait, as you see," Porfiry muttered, putting his ear to the door. And indeed, a commotion could be heard on the other side.
"They're coming!" Raskolnikov cried. "You sent for them! You were expecting them! Well, bring them all out—your deputies, your witnesses, whatever you like! I'm ready!"
But at that moment something strange happened—something so utterly unexpected that neither Raskolnikov nor Porfiry Petrovitch could have foreseen such an ending to their interview.
